es.summary: Infección adquirida durante la estancia hospitalaria que no estaba presente o incubándose al ingreso. Es causada por microorganismos patógenos que se transmiten por contacto directo, superficies o dispositivos invasivos.
key_points: Se produce después de 48 h de hospitalización o tras procedimientos invasivos.
La cadena de infección incluye agente, reservorio, vía de transmisión y huésped susceptible.
La higiene de manos es la medida más eficaz para prevenirla.
El uso prudente de antibióticos reduce la resistencia y el riesgo de infección.
El aislamiento y la desinfección ambiental son esenciales en el control.

pathophysiology: Un microorganismo patógeno coloniza un reservorio (p. ej., piel, dispositivos).
Se transmite al paciente mediante contacto directo, aire o fluidos.
El huésped con factores de riesgo permite la invasión y multiplicación.
Se desencadena una respuesta inflamatoria que puede progresar a sepsis.
risk_factors: Uso de catéteres, ventilación mecánica o sondas.
Uso prolongado de antibióticos de amplio espectro.
Mala higiene de manos del personal y visitantes.
signs_symptoms: Enrojecimiento, calor, dolor y exudado en sitio de catéter o herida.
Escalofríos, taquicardia y aumento de la frecuencia respiratoria.
Cambios en resultados de laboratorio: PCR ↑, procalcitonina ↑.
diagnostics: Cultivo de sangre, orina, exudado o sitio invasivo.
Proteína C‑reactiva y procalcitonina para evaluar inflamación.
Radiografía de tórax o ecografía según sospecha de foco.
treatment: Antibiótico de amplio espectro inicial, ajustado según cultivo.
Control de la fuente: retirar o cambiar catéteres contaminados.
Aislamiento de contacto o gotas según agente identificado.
Reposición de líquidos y soporte hemodinámico si hay sepsis.
Educación al paciente y familia sobre medidas de prevención.
complications: Prolongación de la estancia hospitalaria y mayor mortalidad.
nursing_care: Evaluar signos vitales cada 4 h y observar cambios en temperatura.
Inspeccionar diariamente sitios de catéteres y heridas.
Aplicar técnica aséptica al manipular dispositivos invasivos.
Registrar y reportar cualquier signo de infección al médico.
Mantener aislamiento y uso correcto de EPP (guantes, mascarilla).
Promover hidratación adecuada y nutrición para favorecer la inmunidad.
patient_teaching: Lavado de manos con agua y jabón 20 s o uso de alcohol gel antes y después de contacto.
Informar al personal cualquier enrojecimiento, dolor o secreción.
Completar el ciclo completo de antibióticos aunque mejore.
Evitar tocar o manipular catéteres sin ayuda del personal.
Practicar tos y estornudo cubriendo boca y nariz con pañuelo o codo.

outcomes: Sin signos de infección (temperatura <38 °C, sin enrojecimiento) en 48 h
Higiene de manos adecuada 100 % del tiempo durante la estancia

interventions.action: Mantener el entorno limpio y desinfectar superficies de alto contacto cada 4 h
interventions.rationale: Elimina reservorios potenciales de patógenos

interventions.action: Revisar diariamente la necesidad de catéteres y retirarlos cuando no sean imprescindibles
interventions.rationale: Disminuye la vía de transmisión de infecciones

interventions.action: Colocar señalización de aislamiento cuando sea necesario
interventions.rationale: Facilita la aplicación de precauciones de contacto o gotas

outcomes: Integridad cutánea restaurada sin exudado en 7 días
Reducción del enrojecimiento y dolor a <2/10 en 48 h

interventions.action: Inspeccionar el sitio de inserción del catéter cada 8 h y registrar hallazgos
interventions.rationale: Detecta precozmente signos de infección y permite intervención temprana

interventions.action: Realizar curación estéril con solución salina y apósitos no adherentes
interventions.rationale: Mantiene un ambiente húmedo y reduce la colonización bacteriana

interventions.rationale: Elimina la fuente de contaminación

en.summary: Infection acquired during hospital stay that was not present or incubating at admission. It is caused by pathogenic microorganisms transmitted by direct contact, surfaces or invasive devices.
key_points: Occurs after 48 h of hospitalization or after invasive procedures.
The infection chain includes agent, reservoir, transmission route and susceptible host.
Hand hygiene is the most effective measure to prevent it.
Prudent antibiotic use reduces resistance and infection risk.
Isolation and environmental disinfection are essential for control.

pathophysiology: A pathogenic microorganism colonizes a reservoir (e.g., skin, devices).
It is transmitted to the patient via direct contact, air or fluids.
The host with risk factors allows invasion and multiplication.
An inflammatory response is triggered that may progress to sepsis.
risk_factors: Use of catheters, mechanical ventilation or tubes.
Poor hand hygiene by staff and visitors.
signs_symptoms: Redness, warmth, pain and drainage at catheter or wound site.
Chills, tachycardia and increased respiratory rate.
diagnostics: Blood, urine, exudate or invasive site cultures.
C‑reactive protein and procalcitonin to assess inflammation.
Chest X‑ray or ultrasound as indicated for focus suspicion.
treatment: Initial broad‑spectrum antibiotic, adjusted per culture.
Source control: remove or change contaminated catheters.
Contact or droplet isolation per identified agent.
Fluid resuscitation and hemodynamic support if sepsis present.
Patient and family education on prevention measures.
complications: Prolonged hospital stay and higher mortality.
nursing_care: Assess vital signs every 4 h and monitor temperature changes.
Inspect catheter and wound sites daily.
Apply aseptic technique when handling invasive devices.
Document and report any infection signs to the physician.
Maintain isolation and proper PPE use (gloves, mask).
Promote adequate hydration and nutrition to support immunity.
patient_teaching: Wash hands with soap and water for 20 s or use alcohol gel before and after contact.
Inform staff of any redness, pain or discharge.
Complete the full antibiotic course even if symptoms improve.
Avoid touching or manipulating catheters without staff assistance.
Practice cough and sneeze etiquette by covering mouth and nose with tissue or elbow.

outcomes: No signs of infection (temperature <38 °C, no redness) within 48 h

interventions.action: Teach and supervise hand washing before and after each patient contact
interventions.rationale: Reduces transmission of pathogenic microorganisms

interventions.action: Apply aseptic technique when handling invasive devices
interventions.rationale: Prevents introduction of infectious agents

interventions.action: Keep environment clean and disinfect high‑contact surfaces every 4 h
interventions.rationale: Eliminates potential pathogen reservoirs

interventions.action: Review daily catheter necessity and remove when not essential
interventions.rationale: Reduces transmission route of infections

interventions.action: Place isolation signage when necessary
interventions.rationale: Facilitates contact or droplet precautions

outcomes: Restored skin integrity without drainage in 7 days
Redness and pain reduced to <2/10 within 48 h

interventions.action: Inspect catheter insertion site every 8 h and document findings
interventions.rationale: Detects early infection signs and allows prompt intervention

interventions.action: Perform sterile dressing with saline solution and non‑adherent dressings
interventions.rationale: Maintains a moist environment and reduces bacterial colonization

interventions.action: Change catheter per protocol or when infection signs appear
interventions.rationale: Eliminates contamination source

interventions.action: Administer prescribed antibiotic and monitor clinical response
interventions.rationale: Controls systemic and local infection

interventions.action: Educate patient on importance of not manipulating site and reporting changes
interventions.rationale: Encourages active participation and prevents worsening

key_points.1.quote: The six links are a causative agent, a source, a means of exit from the body, a method of spread, a way into the body, and a susceptible host .

key_points.2.quote: Proper hand washing is the most effective way to prevent the spread of infections in hospitals.

key_points.4.quote: The process of infection control includes handwashing, environmental sanitizing, proper waste management, and adherence to isolation precautions.

sections.pathophysiology.1.quote: Germs can be transmitted via multiple routes, which include direct contact, indirect contact, droplets, the air, water, food, and vectors.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: Factors that increase susceptibility include age, chronic illnesses, a compromised immune system, or immune deficiency.

sections.risk_factors.4.quote: Indirect transmission can occur in a hospital from, for example, ineffective hand hygiene, improper cleaning of medical equipment, and failure to change gloves between patients.

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: A nurse assessing a patient who has a suspected infection will consider findings related to an inflammatory process, such as increased body temperature, heat at the site, redness, or swelling.

sections.treatment.4.quote: If you are a patient, don't be afraid to remind friends, family and health care providers to wash their hands before getting close to you.

sections.complications.0.quote: The body’s extreme response to widespread infection, called sepsis , is the outcome of an inappropriate immune response to an infection that results in function failure in multiple organ systems within the body.

sections.complications.1.quote: The body’s extreme response to widespread infection, called sepsis , is the outcome of an inappropriate immune response to an infection that results in function failure in multiple organ systems within the body.

sections.complications.4.quote: Patients who develop any infection are at risk for prolonged hospital stays, long-term complications, and/or death, but HAIs are specifically dangerous as they are typically resistant to bacterial treatment and spread rapidly to often immunocompromised hospitalized patients.
